How this book matches your exam. This book covers Core Unit 1: Changing population of the IB Geography guide (first assessment 2019):

  • population and economic development patterns;
  • changing populations and places (demographic change, migration);
  • the challenges and opportunities of population change (policies, ageing, gender).

The core is assessed in Paper 2 (SL and HL; 1 hour 15 minutes; 50 marks; 40% (SL) and 25% (HL)).

Unit 1 of 10: Global Population Distribution

Key ideas

  • Population distribution: where people live. Population density: people per km².
  • The world population passed 8 billion in 2022 (UN estimate). The most populous countries are India and China (each with more than 1.4 billion).
  • Distribution is uneven.
  • Densely populated areas: fertile river valleys (the Ganges, the Nile), coasts, temperate climates, economic centres.
  • Sparsely populated areas: deserts, high mountains, polar regions, dense rainforests.
  • Factors:
  • physical: climate, relief, water, soils;
  • human: jobs, infrastructure, history, political factors.

Worked examples

Example 1: Egypt's population is concentrated along the Nile valley and delta, even though most of the country is desert.

Example 2: Canada: most people live within a few hundred kilometres of the US border, where the climate is milder.

Example 3: population density: 10 million people in 50 000 km² = 200 people per km².

10-mark exam-style question

(a) Distinguish between population distribution and population density. [2]

(b) Explain two physical and two human factors that influence population distribution. [8]

Answers:

  • (a) Distribution is the spatial pattern of where people live; density is the number of people per unit area (A2).
  • (b) Physical: water availability (river valleys support farming) (R2); climate (temperate areas are easier to live in than deserts) (R2). Human: employment opportunities in cities attract people (R2); historical and political factors (for example, colonial ports grew into large cities) (R2).

Common mistakes

  1. Mixing up distribution and density.
  2. Out-of-date population figures.
  3. Only physical factors.
  4. No examples.
  5. Calculation errors.

Quick recall

  1. What is population density?
  2. When did the world population reach 8 billion?
  3. Name two densely populated areas.
  4. Name two sparsely populated areas.
  5. What is 10 million ÷ 50 000 km²?

Answers: 1) People per km². 2) 2022. 3) The Ganges valley and the Nile delta. 4) The Sahara and Antarctica. 5) 200 per km².
